query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Q235 steel’s resistance to corrosion in both room‐temperature and high-temperature (700–900 °C) salt exposures is governed by the integrity of its native, amorphous iron oxide passive layer. At room temperature, this passive layer limits corrosion, but under high-temperature salt exposure the layer becomes thermally destabilized, dissolves or transforms into non‐protective phases, thereby accelerating corrosion degradation. An annealing treatment that promotes a more crystalline and thermodynamically stable oxide film should enhance high-temperature corrosion protection.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state featuring a naturally formed, thin, amorphous iron oxide passive layer
generation.intervention: A controlled annealing treatment designed to transform the native amorphous oxide layer into a thicker, more crystalline (and stable) passive film
generation.conditions: Samples will be exposed to an inert environment (as a baseline) and to a corrosive salt environment at room temperature versus high temperatures (700–900 °C). The hypothesis applies in regimes where the passive film remains the primary barrier to corrosion; it may not apply if alloying elements or protective coatings dominate the corrosion behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructure and crystallinity of the surface iron oxide passive film
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, the amorphous passive film affords limited protection by acting as a barrier to corrosive species. Under high-temperature conditions, the inherent instability of this amorphous structure leads to its dissolution or transformation into less protective crystalline forms, greatly increasing metal exposure to salt-induced corrosion. Annealing is predicted to induce a crystalline passive film that resists such phase transformations and dissolution, thereby mitigating corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Untreated Q235 steel is expected to exhibit higher mass loss and more pronounced corrosive damage after high-temperature salt exposure compared to room temperature. In contrast, samples that undergo the annealing treatment should show reduced mass loss and less corrosive degradation at high temperatures relative to the untreated baseline.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel in its original pre-exposure (untreated) state showing established corrosion rates and oxide characteristics at room temperature and under high-temperature salt exposure.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic hypothesis is expected to hold when corrosion is predominantly controlled by the stability of the native iron oxide film. It may not apply if additional alloying elements or coatings—absent in Q235 steel—alter the film formation, or under conditions where corrosion is dominated by non-oxide-related mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative differences in mass loss or corrosion rates between treated and untreated samples under high-temperature conditions are uncertain and need to be calibrated experimentally. The exact phase and morphology of the protective oxide after annealing are also subject to further verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Q235 steel samples: one group remains in the pre-exposure (untreated) state, and the other undergoes a controlled annealing process to promote the formation of a crystalline oxide layer. Expose both groups to a controlled corrosive salt environment at room temperature and at 800 °C for an identical duration. Analyze each sample for mass loss, surface morphology, oxide composition, and phase using SEM, XRD, and gravimetric measurements.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in high-temperature mass loss and display oxide phase and morphology similar to untreated samples (i.e., no improvement in protection), then the hypothesis that thermal destabilization of the native amorphous oxide is the primary driver of corrosion degradation in Q235 steel will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Therefore, in order to investigate the high-temperature protective capabilities of EHEA coatings, AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and AlCoCrFeNi2.1 co-doping with Y and Hf (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding in this paper. After their preparation, the microstructure and high-temperature thermal stability of the coatings were characterized, and the hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% (wt.%) NaCl mixed molten salt was investigated, which provided data support for an evaluation of the potential applications of high-entropy alloy coatings in harsh service environments such as steam pipelines and the hot-end components of gas turbines.

AbstractThe corrosion behavior of the FCC Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 high entropy alloy (HEA) after exposure to molten FLiBe salt at 700 °C for 1000 hours, has been investigated. Results show that the HEA lost a higher mass compared to the reference 316 H stainless steel due to the dissolution of Mn into the molten salt. The loss of Mn from the alloy appeared to discourage the dissolution of Cr in the molten fluoride salts which is widely recognized as the mechanism of corrosion degradation. Thermal exposure at 700 °C for 1000 hours also led to the precipitation of an additional BCC phase Cr67Fe13Mn18.5Ni1.5, which was confirmed by CALPHAD predictions.Subject terms: Structural materials, Metals and alloys

Titanium achieves its excellent corrosion protection because of the high stability of the passive layer that develops on its surface [], which can be re-formed at body temperature and in physiological fluid if it is damaged. The increased popularity of Ti and its alloys as important biomaterials is driven by their low modulus [,,], greater biocompatibility, and better corrosion resistance in comparison to traditional biomaterials, such as stainless steel and Co–Cr alloys []. These desirable qualities were the motivating force for the early insertion of Ti as an implantable material. Ti has low mechanical strength [,], and when aluminum and vanadium are incorporated in low amounts, the resistance of the alloy is greatly improved over that of titanium and the alloy could be successfully used in severe stress situations, such as Ti–6Al–4V, which has been predominantly employed. However, Ti–6Al–4V has significant toxicity; harmful tissue reactions are caused by vanadium and the release of both V and Al ions are related to long-term health disorders such as peripheral neuropathy and Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases [,].
